blocks.text: Amides contain the functional group –CO–NH₂. Since they are prepared from carboxylic acids that is why amides are still sometimes called as “acid amides”.
Amides can be prepared by the following methods.
1. By the reaction of acyl chlorides with ammonia

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + NH3 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH2 + HCl. Below: benzoyl chloride (ring-C(=O)-Cl) + NH3 gives benzamide (ring-C(=O)-NH2) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and ammonia (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

blocks.text: 2. By the reaction of acyl chlorides with primary amines

blocks.alt: CH3-C(=O)-Cl (ethanoyl chloride) + CH3-CH2-NH2 gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-CH2-CH3 (N-ethyl ethanamide) + HCl. Below: CH3-C(=O)-Cl + phenyl amine gives CH3-C(=O)-NH-ring (N-phenyl ethanamide) + HCl.
blocks.caption: Amides from acyl chlorides and primary amines (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 127).

blocks.text: In the above two methods, all the reactions take place at room temperature, releasing white fumes of hydrogen chloride (HCl). The HCl produced reacts with another molecule of ammonia or amine to form a salt.

All amides except methanamide, which is a liquid, are solid with sharp melting point. They have quite high boiling points which is a consequence of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding. However, in case of N-substituted amides, the melting and boiling points decrease as the sites for hydrogen bonding diminish with increasing number of alkyl substituents.

blocks.alt: R-NH2 + HCl gives R-NH3(+) Cl(-). Below: NH3 + HCl gives NH4(+) Cl(-).
blocks.caption: Salt formation by an amine and by ammonia with HCl (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 128).

blocks.text: Therefore, an excess of ammonia or amine is used to ensure complete reaction.
